newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Top futures exchanges link up ahead of EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Top futures exchanges link up ahead of EMU.

text.p: Europe's top two financial exchanges linked up with the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME) on Wednesday, carving up business among them ahead of a single European currency.
The London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) said it signed a deal with the CME to link trade in short-term interest rate futures and options contracts.
At the same time, French futures and options exchange Matif signed an accord with the CME which begins with Matif's French bond future and will apply to all contracts of one year or more.

"We are very satisfied with this agreement which constitutes an important milestone in our committed strategy of preparation for monetary union and confirms the view of MATIF as the market leader in euro products," said Gerard Pfauwald, president of MATIF.
Financial exchanges have been jostling for position ahead of the planned launch of single currency under European economic and monetary union (EMU), due to start in 1999.
Market participants said LIFFE's case for being a primary exchange for euro contracts would be strengthened by a link with another major exchange.
"LIFFE is trying to ensure they will be integral in a post EMU world, even if the UK is out," said a director of a U.S. futures house in London.

The LIFFE link will start with three-month Euromark futures, as part of arrangement whereby LIFFE's own short-term interest rate futures and options can be traded on CME after LIFFE has closed, extending the trading day for the LIFFE contracts.

"The Euromark is the most liquid short-term interest rate future in Europe and will settle against euros if EMU goes ahead. The link strengthens the contract and will distribute this benchmark instrument in the American time zone," LIFFE chairman Jack Wigglesworth said in a statement.
A link between LIFFE and the Chicago Board of Trade is already under development, and after an initial postponement as a result of technical difficulties, is scheduled for a May 9 1997 start date.
On Tuesday, the exchanges announced that the link would be amended to include trading long-dated euro debt products in its open outcry pits.
However, traders said the drive for link-ups may have been driven by LIFFE's plans to position itself for EMU, rather than by investor demand.

"Lengthening the hours will just spread existing liquidity over a longer time period," said a broker at a major brokerage on the LIFFE floor. "I'll be interested to see what kind of business this will generate from the U.S."
Wigglesworth denied this, saying the drive for the venture came from members.

"This move will significantly increase volume," Jack Wigglesworth, chairman of LIFFE said. "Our members want this. There is strong D-mark cash business in north America and we will see deepening liquidity."
MATIF said its agreement was initially for five years.

While the 10-year French franc bond future and options contracts will be the first to trade, MATIF products with "a maturity of more than one year, denominated in francs, Ecu, the euro, or any other European currency," are also covered.

Wigglesworth said LIFFE was in constant contact with other exchanges around the world, although he said it was not easy to establish joint-ventures with those in the same time zone without splitting liquidity.
